The chunk measures the effect: a perceptron is trained on the glyphs in their usual positions and tested on a fresh set of glyphs displaced by one, two and three pixels.

shift_flat <- function(X, dx, dy) t(apply(X, 1, function(v) as.vector(shift_img(matrix(v,SG,SG), dx, dy))))
set.seed(20); Gte <- make_glyphs(40)                       # fresh held-out glyphs
raw_mlp <- nnet(Gs, class.ind(G$y), size=16, softmax=TRUE, maxit=250, trace=FALSE, decay=1e-3, MaxNWts=1e5)
shifts <- list(c(0,0),c(1,0),c(0,1),c(1,1),c(2,0),c(2,2),c(3,0))
acc_raw <- sapply(shifts, function(s) mean(predict(raw_mlp, scale(shift_flat(Gte$X,s[1],s[2]),Gctr,Gsd), type="class")==Gte$y))
cat("test accuracy when the glyphs are shifted by (dx,dy):\n")
## test accuracy when the glyphs are shifted by (dx,dy):
cat(paste(sapply(seq_along(shifts), function(i) sprintf("(%d,%d):%.3f", shifts[[i]][1], shifts[[i]][2], acc_raw[i])), collapse="  "), "\n")
## (0,0):0.933  (1,0):0.783  (0,1):0.758  (1,1):0.596  (2,0):0.438  (2,2):0.179  (3,0):0.204
k <- which(predict(raw_mlp, Gs, type="class")==G$y & G$y=="cross")[1]
par(mfrow=c(1,6), mar=c(1,1,2.4,1))
for (i in 1:5){ s <- shifts[[i]]; im <- shift_img(matrix(G$X[k,],SG,SG), s[1], s[2])
  pr <- predict(raw_mlp, scale(matrix(as.vector(im),1), Gctr, Gsd), type="class")
  image(t(im[SG:1,]), col=grey.colors(32,1,0), axes=FALSE); title(sprintf("shift (%d,%d)\nsaid %s", s[1],s[2],substr(pr,1,4)), cex.main=0.8); box() }
barplot(acc_raw, names.arg=sapply(shifts,function(s)paste0("(",s[1],",",s[2],")")), col=palette_neg,
        ylim=c(0,1), las=2, cex.names=0.6, main="accuracy vs shift", cex.main=0.8)

Figure 14. Left: a held-out glyph displaced by up to two pixels, with the perceptron’s prediction under each. Right: test accuracy as a function of the shift. The unshifted accuracy is high; a displacement of one pixel — one eighth of the image — already lowers it, and two or three pixels drive it towards chance. Nothing about the glyphs changed; only their position did. A radiograph is never positioned to the pixel, and a lesion can appear anywhere in the field of view, so this fragility would be disqualifying in practice. Section 2.3 offers one remedy, augmentation with shifted copies; Section 6.4 measures how far it goes and introduces the second remedy, which is architectural.

6.2 Convolution, by hand

A convolution slides a small matrix of weights — the kernel or filter, typically 3 × 3 — over the image and, at each position, outputs the sum of the products of the kernel entries with the pixels under them:

\[(\mathbf{I} \star \mathbf{K})_{r,c} = \sum_{u=1}^{k} \sum_{v=1}^{k} K_{u,v}\, I_{r+u-1,\, c+v-1}\] The output is a feature map: large where the image locally resembles the kernel. At the image border the missing neighbours are filled by zero padding (“same” output size) or dropped (“valid”, smaller output). Strictly this operation is a cross-correlation; a mathematical convolution flips the kernel first. Deep-learning libraries compute the cross-correlation and call it convolution, and since the kernels are learned the distinction is immaterial. Without padding, a \(k \times k\) kernel on an \(H \times W\) image gives an \((H-k+1) \times (W-k+1)\) map.

The same nine weights are applied at every position: the kernel is a single template shared across the image, in contrast to the 64 independent weights per unit of the perceptron. That weight sharing is what gives the operation translation equivariance — shift the image and the feature map shifts with it, unchanged otherwise — and the pooling step that follows converts equivariance into (local) invariance. Take a 4 × 4 image with a vertical edge in its upper half and the vertical-edge kernel \(\mathbf{K}\):

\[\mathbf{I} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 5 & 5 \\ 1 & 1 & 5 & 5 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{K} = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\]

The valid output is 2 × 2. At position (1,1) the window is the top-left 3 × 3 block; each of its rows contributes \(-1 \cdot (\text{left}) + 0 + 1 \cdot (\text{right})\): rows 1 and 2 give \(-1 + 5 = 4\) each, row 3 gives \(-1 + 1 = 0\), total \(8\). At (1,2) the window moves one column right: rows 1 and 2 give \(-1 + 5 = 4\), row 3 gives \(0\), total \(8\). At (2,1) the window covers rows 2–4: row 2 gives \(4\), rows 3 and 4 give \(0\), total \(4\); at (2,2) likewise \(4\). So \(\mathbf{I} \star \mathbf{K} = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} 8 & 8 \\ 4 & 4 \end{smallmatrix}\right)\). With the transposed kernel (a horizontal-edge detector) position (1,1) gives \(-(1+1+5) + (1+1+1) = -4\) and position (1,2) gives \(-(1+5+5) + 3 = -8\); the second row repeats them. A ReLU sets the negative responses to zero, so this image excites the vertical-edge map and not the horizontal one; a 2 × 2 max-pooling of the vertical map returns the single number 8 — “there is a vertical edge somewhere in this image”, regardless of where. The chunk confirms the numbers.

conv_valid <- function(I, K){ k <- nrow(K); H <- nrow(I); W <- ncol(I)
  outer(1:(H-k+1), 1:(W-k+1), Vectorize(function(r,c) sum(K * I[r:(r+k-1), c:(c+k-1)]))) }
maxpool <- function(M, s=2){ H <- nrow(M)/s; W <- ncol(M)/s
  outer(1:H,1:W, Vectorize(function(r,c) max(M[((r-1)*s+1):(r*s),((c-1)*s+1):(c*s)]))) }
Iv <- matrix(c(1,1,5,5, 1,1,5,5, 1,1,1,1, 1,1,1,1), 4, 4, byrow=TRUE)
Kv <- matrix(c(-1,0,1, -1,0,1, -1,0,1), 3, 3, byrow=TRUE)
mv <- conv_valid(Iv, Kv); mh <- conv_valid(Iv, t(Kv))
cat("vertical-edge map:\n"); print(mv); cat("horizontal-edge map:\n"); print(mh)
## vertical-edge map:
##      [,1] [,2]
## [1,]    8    8
## [2,]    4    4
## horizontal-edge map:
##      [,1] [,2]
## [1,]   -4   -8
## [2,]   -4   -8
cat("after ReLU + 2x2 max-pool -> vertical:", as.vector(maxpool(pmax(mv,0))),
    " horizontal:", as.vector(maxpool(pmax(mh,0))), "\n")
## after ReLU + 2x2 max-pool -> vertical: 8  horizontal: 0

The code reproduces the hand result — \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix} 8 & 8 \\ 4 & 4 \end{smallmatrix}\right)\) for the vertical kernel and \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix} -4 & -8 \\ -4 & -8 \end{smallmatrix}\right)\) for the horizontal one. After the ReLU and the pooling, the image is summarised by two numbers, 8 and 0: “a vertical edge, no horizontal edge”.

6.3 Feature maps and pooling on real images

The chunk applies a small bank of fixed filters — vertical and horizontal Sobel edge detectors, a Laplacian (responds to points and thin lines), a Gaussian blur, and a difference-of-Gaussians “blob” detector tuned to the size of the simulated nodules — to a glyph and to a nodule patch, with “same” padding, and shows the maps before and after 4 × 4 max-pooling.

FILTERS <- list(
  `Sobel v`=matrix(c(-1,0,1,-2,0,2,-1,0,1),3,3,byrow=TRUE),
  `Sobel h`=matrix(c(-1,-2,-1,0,0,0,1,2,1),3,3,byrow=TRUE),
  Laplacian=matrix(c(0,-1,0,-1,4,-1,0,-1,0),3,3,byrow=TRUE),
  blur=gkern(1.0,3), blob=gkern(1.2,9)-gkern(2.4,9))
feature_maps <- function(img) lapply(FILTERS, function(K) pmax(conv_same(img,K),0))
set.seed(7); gl <- draw_glyph("diagL"); pt <- nod$X[which(nod$y==1)[1],,]
par(mfrow=c(4,6), mar=c(0.4,0.4,1.4,0.4), oma=c(0,0,2,0))
for (ex in list(list(gl,"glyph"), list(pt,"nodule patch"))){ maps <- feature_maps(ex[[1]])
  image(t(ex[[1]][nrow(ex[[1]]):1,]),col=grey.colors(32,1,0),axes=FALSE,main=ex[[2]],cex.main=0.85); box()   # row: original + maps
  for (nm in names(FILTERS)){ M <- maps[[nm]]; image(t(M[nrow(M):1,]),col=hcl.colors(32,"Inferno"),axes=FALSE,main=nm,cex.main=0.85); box() }
  plot.new()                                                                                                  # row: blank + pooled maps
  for (nm in names(FILTERS)){ Mp <- maxpool(maps[[nm]],4); image(t(Mp[nrow(Mp):1,]),col=hcl.colors(32,"Inferno"),axes=FALSE,main="pooled",cex.main=0.8); box() } }
mtext("Feature maps (ReLU of the correlation) and, below each, its 4x4 max-pool", outer=TRUE, line=0.3, cex=0.9, font=2)

cat("map sizes: patch 16x16 -> pooled", paste(dim(maxpool(feature_maps(pt)[[1]],4)), collapse=" x "), "\n")
## map sizes: patch 16x16 -> pooled 4 x 4

Figure 15. Columns 1 and (per block) the originals; the remaining columns are the five feature maps and, beneath each, its 4 × 4 max-pooled version, for a glyph (first two rows) and a nodule patch (last two rows). The Sobel maps light up on edges according to their orientation; the Laplacian responds to thin structures and noise; the blur map is a smoothed copy; the blob detector responds strongly and selectively to the nodule and weakly to the background texture — it is a template of “a bright round object about this size” applied at every position. Pooling discards the exact position within each 4 × 4 block while keeping the information that the feature was present: a nodule displaced by one or two pixels lands in the same pooled cell. Stacking convolution, non-linearity and pooling several times, with the kernels learned by backpropagation rather than fixed, is the convolutional neural network of LeCun and colleagues,[14] and the one that won ImageNet in 2012.[16]

6.4 A minimal convolutional front end, and the return of shift robustness

The chunk assembles the pieces into a fixed-filter convolutional front end: the filter bank, a ReLU, 4 × 4 max-pooling, and the per-map global maximum and mean, followed by a perceptron on the resulting vector. Nothing in the front end is learned — the filters are the hand-designed ones above — so this is not a convolutional network in the full sense; it is a demonstration that the structure of convolution and pooling, not only the learning of the filters, is what buys robustness. The experiment repeats the shift test for four systems: the raw perceptron; the raw perceptron trained with shift augmentation; the convolutional front end; and the front end with augmentation.

conv_features <- function(X, pool=4){ t(apply(X, 1, function(v){ maps <- feature_maps(matrix(v,SG,SG))
  c(unlist(lapply(maps, function(M) as.vector(maxpool(M,pool)))),
    sapply(maps, max), sapply(maps, mean)) })) }
aug_shifts <- list(c(1,0),c(-1,0),c(0,1),c(0,-1))
Xaug <- rbind(G$X, do.call(rbind, lapply(aug_shifts, function(s) shift_flat(G$X,s[1],s[2])))); yaug <- rep(G$y, 5)
fit_eval <- function(Xtr,ytr,featfun){ Z <- featfun(Xtr); ce <- colMeans(Z); s <- apply(Z,2,sd); s[s==0] <- 1
  fit <- nnet(scale(Z,ce,s), class.ind(ytr), size=16, softmax=TRUE, maxit=200, trace=FALSE, decay=1e-3, MaxNWts=1e5)
  function(Xte) mean(predict(fit, scale(featfun(Xte),ce,s), type="class")==Gte$y) }
idf <- function(X) X
systems <- list(`raw pixels`=fit_eval(G$X,G$y,idf),
                `raw + shift aug`=fit_eval(Xaug,yaug,idf),
                `conv front end`=fit_eval(G$X,G$y,conv_features),
                `conv + aug`=fit_eval(Xaug,yaug,conv_features))
tab <- sapply(systems, function(ev) sapply(shifts[c(1,2,5,7)], function(s) round(ev(shift_flat(Gte$X,s[1],s[2])),3)))
rownames(tab) <- sapply(shifts[c(1,2,5,7)], function(s) sprintf("shift (%d,%d)",s[1],s[2]))
cat("features per image: raw", ncol(G$X), "| conv front end", ncol(conv_features(G$X[1:2,])), "\n")
## features per image: raw 64 | conv front end 30
print(t(tab))
##                 shift (0,0) shift (1,0) shift (2,0) shift (3,0)
## raw pixels            0.938       0.812       0.446       0.275
## raw + shift aug       0.892       0.842       0.542       0.271
## conv front end        0.900       0.783       0.596       0.342
## conv + aug            0.858       0.829       0.708       0.442

Read the table row by row. The raw perceptron falls off quickly with the shift. Augmentation repairs mainly the shifts it was shown — one pixel in each direction — and helps less at larger displacements: the network memorised a few extra positions; it did not learn that position is irrelevant. The convolutional front end alone, with fixed filters and one pooling stage, is more robust because 4 × 4 pooling tolerates a displacement while the feature stays in the same block. The combination is the most robust at the larger shifts: the pooled representation makes a shifted glyph look similar to the network, so the invariance learned from small examples extrapolates to shifts it never saw. That extrapolation is what an inductive bias is — an assumption built into the architecture that lets the model generalise beyond the cases in the sample — and it is why convolutional networks learned from thousands of radiographs what perceptrons could not learn from millions of pixels.

From this front end to deep learning, and to transfer learning

A real convolutional network differs from the chunk above in three ways. Its filters are learned by backpropagation together with the classifier, so the blob detector we tuned by hand is discovered from data — and so are detectors nobody thought to design. It stacks several convolution–ReLU–pooling blocks, so that later layers combine edges into parts and parts into objects. And it is trained on far more images than a hospital has — which is why transfer learning is the standard recipe in medical imaging: a network pre-trained on the 1.2 million natural images of ImageNet[16] has its last layer replaced and is fine-tuned on a few thousand medical images. Shin and colleagues showed that filters learned on photographs transfer usefully to CT, because edges, blobs and textures are universal;[17] every landmark paper of Section 8 used it. This notebook does not run a deep network, because the course uses no deep-learning framework; MedMNIST[8] with a framework such as Keras or Torch is the place to do so afterwards.

6.5 The same lesson on the simulated patches

The patches allow a complementary experiment that the glyphs cannot: the position of the lesion is a parameter of the generator. The chunk generates three nodule datasets in which the lesion centre is jittered by up to 1, 3 and 6 pixels around the centre of the 16 × 16 patch, and cross-validates the same perceptron on three representations — raw pixels, the 14 hand-crafted features of Section 3, and the convolutional front end with the blob detector.

conv_feat_patch <- function(X, pool=4){ t(apply(X, 1, function(v){ img <- matrix(v,SIZE,SIZE)
  maps <- lapply(FILTERS, function(K) pmax(conv_same(img,K),0))
  c(sapply(maps, max), sapply(maps, mean), unlist(lapply(maps, function(M) as.vector(maxpool(M,pool))))) })) }
jitters <- c(1,3,6); reps <- list()
for (j in jitters){ set.seed(20+j); pj <- make_patches(500, "nodule", jitter=j)
  Pp <- flat_patch(pj$X); Fp <- t(sapply(1:500, function(k) extract_features(pj$X[k,,]))); Cp <- conv_feat_patch(pj$X)
  fo <- strat_folds(pj$y, 3)
  for (rep in c("raw pixels","14 features","conv front end")){ Xin <- switch(rep, `raw pixels`=Pp, `14 features`=Fp, Cp)
    p <- mlp_bin_cv(Xin, pj$y, 4, fo, 0.5)
    a <- sapply(1:3, function(f){ te <- fo==f; mean((p[te]>0.5)==pj$y[te]) })
    reps[[rep]] <- rbind(reps[[rep]], c(mean(a), sd(a))) } }
cols <- c(palette_neg, palette_acc, palette_pos)
plot(NA, xlim=range(jitters), ylim=c(0.5,1), xlab="max lesion displacement (pixels)", ylab="CV accuracy",
     main="Nodule task: three representations vs lesion position"); i <- 1
for (rep in names(reps)){ m <- reps[[rep]]; lines(jitters, m[,1], type="b", pch=19, col=cols[i])
  arrows(jitters, m[,1]-m[,2], jitters, m[,1]+m[,2], angle=90, code=3, length=0.03, col=cols[i]); i <- i+1 }
legend("bottomleft", names(reps), col=cols, lwd=2, pch=19, bty="n", cex=0.8)

for (rep in names(reps)) cat(sprintf("%-16s %s\n", rep, paste(sprintf("%.3f+/-%.3f", reps[[rep]][,1], reps[[rep]][,2]), collapse="  ")))
## raw pixels       0.942+/-0.004  0.698+/-0.039  0.612+/-0.043
## 14 features      0.894+/-0.003  0.896+/-0.046  0.912+/-0.009
## conv front end   0.964+/-0.012  0.936+/-0.015  0.878+/-0.012

Figure 16. Cross-validated accuracy of the same perceptron on three representations of the nodule patches, as the lesion is allowed to wander further from the centre. On raw pixels the network degrades as the nodule can be anywhere: it has to learn a separate template for every position, and five hundred images are not enough. The hand-crafted features are invariant by construction — area, contrast and texture do not depend on where the blob is — and their curve is the flattest. The convolutional front end sits between the two: its blob detector is applied everywhere and its pooling discards position within 4 × 4 blocks, so it degrades gracefully; a network with learned filters and more pooling stages would be flatter still. The figure is the whole argument of the section in one picture: with little data, invariance must come from somewhere other than the data — from designed features or from the architecture.

Exercise 4

Change pool=4 to pool=16 in conv_feat_patch, so that every map is reduced to a single global maximum and mean. The representation is now fully translation-invariant; is it still discriminative? Then run the microcalcification set (mc) through the same three representations. Which filter of the bank carries the signal for that task, and why do the first-order features fail on it?

7. What can go wrong in medical image classification

7.1 Shortcut learning: the network learns the hospital

Unit 1 simulated a scanner identifier that predicted the label in the training hospital and not elsewhere. With images the confound need not be a separate column: it can be in the pixels. Zech and colleagues trained a convolutional network to detect pneumonia on radiographs pooled from several hospitals and found that it identified the source hospital from the image with near-perfect accuracy — from laterality markers, burnt-in text, the field of view — and used the hospital’s pneumonia prevalence as a predictor, so that its external performance was far below its internal cross-validation.[18] Geirhos and colleagues named the phenomenon shortcut learning: the model finds the easiest regularity that predicts the label in the training distribution, intended or not.[19] DeGrave and colleagues showed that the COVID-19 radiograph detectors of 2020 — positives from one set of sources, negatives from another — relied on markers, image borders and shoulder position rather than on the lungs.[20] The chunk reproduces the mechanism with hospital A, whose positive patches carry a corner marker 90 % of the time, and evaluates the perceptron on new patches from the same hospital and from a hospital B without markers.

fit_pix <- function(X, y){ ce <- colMeans(X); s <- apply(X,2,sd); s[s==0] <- 1
  m <- nnet(scale(X,ce,s), y, size=6, entropy=TRUE, maxit=250, trace=FALSE, decay=0.5, MaxNWts=1e5)
  function(Xn) as.vector(predict(m, scale(Xn,ce,s))) }
set.seed(10); XA <- make_patches(1000, "nodule", hospital="A", marker_rate=0.9)   # training hospital
set.seed(11); XA2 <- make_patches(400, "nodule", hospital="A", marker_rate=0.9)   # new cases, same hospital
set.seed(12); XB <- make_patches(400, "nodule", hospital="B")                     # another hospital, no markers
set.seed(13); XH <- make_patches(1000, "nodule", hospital="B")                    # a marker-free training set
mA <- fit_pix(flat_patch(XA$X), XA$y); mH <- fit_pix(flat_patch(XH$X), XH$y)
ev <- function(m, d) mean((m(flat_patch(d$X))>0.5)==d$y)
res <- rbind(`trained at hospital A (marker)` = c(`training`=ev(mA,XA), `new, same hospital`=ev(mA,XA2), `new, hospital B`=ev(mA,XB)),
             `trained without markers`         = c(ev(mH,XH), ev(mH,XA2), ev(mH,XB)))
cat(sprintf("fraction of hospital-A positives carrying the marker: %.2f\n",
            mean(apply(XA$X[XA$y==1,,], 1, function(im) all(im[2:3,(SIZE-3):(SIZE-1)]>0.9)))))
## fraction of hospital-A positives carrying the marker: 0.89
print(round(res,3))
##                                training new, same hospital new, hospital B
## trained at hospital A (marker)        1              0.953            0.66
## trained without markers               1              0.815            0.86

The model trained at hospital A looks excellent at home — its accuracy on new cases from the same hospital is well above that of the marker-free model, because the marker is a far easier cue than a faint nodule — and loses many points at hospital B, where it must rely on whatever it learned about nodules, which is less than the marker-free model learned. As in Unit 1, no internal number warned of the failure: training accuracy and same-hospital accuracy were both high. The cause can be made visible, which is the subject of the next section.

7.2 Where is the network looking? Occlusion sensitivity

A saliency map shows which parts of an image drive a prediction. The simplest, introduced by Zeiler and Fergus, is occlusion sensitivity: cover a small square of the image with a neutral value, record how much the predicted probability of the class drops, move the square, and repeat; the map of drops shows where the evidence is.[21] It requires nothing but the ability to call the model’s probability output, so it works for a perceptron as well as for a deep network. The drop is measured in log-odds, \(\log[p/(1-p)]\), rather than in probability, because a confident model outputs \(p \approx 1\) for many patches and a drop from 0.999 to 0.99 — a ten-fold change in the odds — would be invisible on the probability scale. The chunk computes it for the two models of Section 7.1 on three positive hospital-A patches that carry the marker.

logit <- function(p){ p <- pmin(pmax(p,1e-6),1-1e-6); log(p/(1-p)) }
occ_map <- function(model, img, size=5, step=2){ base <- model(matrix(as.vector(t(img)),1))
  H <- matrix(0,SIZE,SIZE); N <- matrix(0,SIZE,SIZE)
  for (r in seq(1,SIZE-size+1,step)) for (c in seq(1,SIZE-size+1,step)){ oc <- img; oc[r:(r+size-1),c:(c+size-1)] <- mean(img)
    d <- logit(base) - logit(model(matrix(as.vector(t(oc)),1)))
    H[r:(r+size-1),c:(c+size-1)] <- H[r:(r+size-1),c:(c+size-1)] + d; N[r:(r+size-1),c:(c+size-1)] <- N[r:(r+size-1),c:(c+size-1)] + 1 }
  list(map=H/pmax(N,1), p=base) }
idx <- which(XA2$y==1 & apply(XA2$X, 1, function(im) im[2,SIZE-2]>0.9))[1:3]
par(mfrow=c(3,3), mar=c(1,1,2.6,1), oma=c(0,0,2.4,0))
for (i in idx){ om_s <- occ_map(mA, XA2$X[i,,]); om_h <- occ_map(mH, XA2$X[i,,])
  image(t(XA2$X[i,,][SIZE:1,]), col=grey.colors(32,1,0), axes=FALSE, zlim=c(0,1))
  title(sprintf("p=%.2f (A-model)\n%.2f (marker-free)", om_s$p, om_h$p), cex.main=0.85); box()
  for (om in list(list(om_s,"hospital-A model"), list(om_h,"marker-free model"))){ v <- max(abs(om[[1]]$map))+1e-9
    image(t(om[[1]]$map[SIZE:1,]), col=colorRampPalette(c(palette_neg,"white",palette_pos))(32), axes=FALSE, zlim=c(-v,v))
    title(sprintf("%s\nmax drop %.1f", om[[2]], max(om[[1]]$map)), cex.main=0.85); box() } }
mtext("Occlusion sensitivity (orange: covering this region lowers the log-odds of 'nodule')", outer=TRUE, line=0.4, cex=0.9, font=2)

Figure 17. Three positive patches from hospital A (left) and the occlusion-sensitivity maps of the two models. For the model trained at hospital A (middle) the evidence is the corner marker: covering the top-right corner collapses the probability, and covering the nodule changes little. For the marker-free model (right) the evidence is the nodule itself. The maps are coarse — the occluder is 5 × 5 pixels moved in steps of 2 — but they would have revealed the shortcut before deployment, which is how the markers and borders of the COVID-19 detectors were found.[20] Saliency maps have limits of their own: they show where the model looked, not why, they can be noisy, and a map that highlights the lesion does not prove that the model has understood it. Used as a debugging tool, as here, they are indispensable.

The shortcut need not be a marker

Any variable that correlates with the label in the training sample and is visible in the pixels can be a shortcut: the scanner model (through noise texture), the department (portable radiographs are taken on sicker patients), the presence of a chest drain in pneumothorax images — a case documented by Oakden-Rayner and colleagues, whose network detected the treatment rather than the condition[22] — or the ruler placed next to lesions that dermatologists already suspect. The defence is the one Unit 1 gave: evaluate on data from a different site, stratify the evaluation by every variable that could be a shortcut, and look at saliency maps of the errors and of the confident successes.

7.3 Class imbalance, prevalence and label noise

Two properties of real imaging datasets that the balanced simulations hide deserve an experiment each. Class imbalance: in screening, positives are rare, and a classifier trained on 95 % negatives learns that “negative” is a good answer; its accuracy is high and its sensitivity is low. The simplest remedy is often to keep the model and move the threshold, as Section 4.5 did. Label noise: the labels of the large radiograph datasets were extracted from reports by text mining and are wrong in a known fraction of cases;[3] the survey of Frénay and Verleysen reviews what noise does to classifiers.[23] Two things happen: the model learns worse, and — more insidiously — the measured accuracy on a noisily labelled test set is capped below the true accuracy, so a perfect model looks imperfect.

set.seed(30); Xneg <- make_patches(950, "nodule", positive=FALSE); set.seed(31); Xpos <- make_patches(50, "nodule", positive=TRUE)
Xi <- rbind(flat_patch(Xneg$X), flat_patch(Xpos$X)); Fi <- rbind(t(sapply(1:950,function(k)extract_features(Xneg$X[k,,]))),
                                                                 t(sapply(1:50,function(k)extract_features(Xpos$X[k,,]))))
yi <- c(rep(0,950), rep(1,50)); set.seed(0); foi <- strat_folds(yi, 5)
pi_oof <- mlp_bin_cv(Fi, yi, 6, foi, 0.5)
roc_i <- roc(yi, pi_oof, quiet=TRUE, direction="<")
t90 <- coords(roc_i, x=0.90, input="sensitivity", ret="threshold")[1,1]
metrics <- function(pred) c(accuracy=mean(pred==yi), sensitivity=mean(pred[yi==1]), specificity=1-mean(pred[yi==0]), `positives called`=sum(pred))
res_i <- rbind(`always negative`=metrics(rep(0,length(yi))), `MLP, threshold 0.5`=metrics(as.integer(pi_oof>=0.5)),
               `MLP, threshold for 90% sens`=metrics(as.integer(pi_oof>=t90)))
cat(sprintf("prevalence %.1f%% | ROC-AUC %.3f | threshold for 90%% sensitivity %.2f\n", 100*mean(yi), as.numeric(auc(roc_i)), t90))
## prevalence 5.0% | ROC-AUC 0.949 | threshold for 90% sensitivity 0.06
print(round(res_i,3))
##                             accuracy sensitivity specificity positives called
## always negative                0.950        0.00       1.000                0
## MLP, threshold 0.5             0.986        0.74       0.999               38
## MLP, threshold for 90% sens    0.930        0.90       0.932              110

The trivial rule that calls everything negative has an accuracy of 0.95 — the prevalence of negatives — and a sensitivity of zero. The perceptron on the hand-crafted features does better than that at the default threshold and still misses a share of the nodules, because with 50 positives among 1,000 the cheapest way to reduce the training loss is to be conservative; the ROC-AUC shows that its probabilities rank the cases well. Lowering the threshold to the value that reaches 90 % sensitivity recovers most of the missed cases at the cost of more positive calls and a lower accuracy. On an imbalanced task accuracy is not a measure of anything useful (Supplement S1); sensitivity, specificity, the ROC curve and, for the clinician, the PPV at the deployment prevalence are.

set.seed(40); tr <- sample(nrow(G$X), round(0.7*nrow(G$X))); levs <- GLYPHS
flip_labels <- function(y, q){ y <- as.character(y); fl <- runif(length(y))<q
  y[fl] <- sapply(which(fl), function(i) sample(setdiff(levs, y[i]), 1)); factor(y, levels=levs) }
qs <- c(0,0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4); clean_acc <- noisy_acc <- numeric(length(qs))
for (k in seq_along(qs)){ set.seed(40+k); ytr <- flip_labels(G$y[tr], qs[k]); yte_n <- flip_labels(G$y[-tr], qs[k])
  fit <- nnet(Gs[tr,], class.ind(ytr), size=24, softmax=TRUE, maxit=200, trace=FALSE, decay=1e-3, MaxNWts=1e5)
  pr <- predict(fit, Gs[-tr,], type="class"); clean_acc[k] <- mean(pr==G$y[-tr]); noisy_acc[k] <- mean(pr==yte_n) }
plot(qs, clean_acc, type="b", pch=19, col=palette_neg, ylim=c(0.3,1.02), xlab="fraction of flipped training labels",
     ylab="test accuracy", main="Label noise on the glyphs")
lines(qs, noisy_acc, type="b", pch=15, lty=2, col=palette_pos); lines(qs, 1-qs, lty=3, col="grey40")
legend("bottomleft", c("vs CLEAN labels","vs equally NOISY labels","ceiling 1 - q"),
       col=c(palette_neg,palette_pos,"grey40"), lty=c(1,2,3), pch=c(19,15,NA), bty="n", cex=0.75)

cat("clean-label accuracy:", round(clean_acc,3), "| noisy-label accuracy:", round(noisy_acc,3), "\n")
## clean-label accuracy: 0.907 0.824 0.759 0.542 0.519 | noisy-label accuracy: 0.907 0.782 0.625 0.449 0.361

Figure 18. Test accuracy of the glyph perceptron as the fraction of flipped training labels grows, measured against clean test labels (blue) and against test labels corrupted at the same rate (orange). The blue curve degrades gradually, because wrong labels spread over the other classes partly cancel out; with more training images the curve would be flatter. The orange curve is the one a researcher with noisy labels would actually see: it runs below the grey ceiling \(1-q\) by about the model’s true error, so a model that is in fact accurate is reported as far worse at high noise. Noise that is systematic — a report-mining rule that always misses one kind of pneumonia — is not averaged out and is far more damaging; the uncertainty labels of CheXpert[4] and the radiologist-adjudicated test sets of the landmark papers exist because of this.

7.4 External validation, reader studies and the regulatory status of imaging AI

Three practices separate a model that works in a notebook from a device that works in a hospital. External validation evaluates the frozen model on data from institutions, scanners and periods that contributed nothing to its development; the CLAIM checklist for AI in medical imaging makes it a reporting requirement, together with the sample, the reference standard, the pre-processing, the model-selection procedure and metrics with confidence intervals.[24] A reader study compares the model with clinicians reading the same cases under the same conditions, ideally also reading with the model, because the deployed system is the combination. Prospective evaluation measures what happens to patients when the model is used.

The regulatory record shows how rarely these are done. Benjamens and colleagues catalogued 64 AI-based devices cleared or approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration by 2020, the majority in radiology, and found that most public summaries disclosed little about the evaluation.[25] Wu and colleagues examined 130 such devices: 126 had been evaluated only retrospectively, 93 reported no multi-site evaluation, and few reported performance by demographic subgroup.[26] Most are software as a medical device cleared through the 510(k) pathway by equivalence to an existing device, not through clinical trials; the framework of Unit 1 — the European AI Act’s high-risk classification, the FDA’s good-machine-learning-practice principles, the WHO’s six principles — is the context in which the engineer’s choices in this unit become legal obligations.

8. Reading the landmark papers

The papers below defined the field between 2016 and 2020 and are the ones your Workshop 2 presentations are most likely to cite. For each, the questions of Unit 1 are asked: what were the objects, the labels and their reference standard, the sample, the metric, the comparator — and what is missing. The table is a reading guide, not a substitute for the papers.

Paper Task and data Headline result Comparator What to ask
Gulshan et al., JAMA 2016[27] Referable diabetic retinopathy on 128,175 retinal photographs, each graded by several of 54 ophthalmologists; validated on two sets of 9,963 and 1,748 images AUC about 0.99 on both; at the high-sensitivity operating point, sensitivity about 97 % and specificity about 93 % Majority vote of ophthalmologists as reference standard Retrospective; images from the cameras and populations of the training sites; ungradeable images excluded; no patient outcome
Esteva et al., Nature 2017[28] Skin lesions: a network pre-trained on ImageNet and fine-tuned on 129,450 clinical images of 2,032 diseases; tested on biopsy-proven images Sensitivity–specificity at or above the operating points of 21 dermatologists on three binary tasks 21 board-certified dermatologists reading the same images Dermatologists read photographs, not patients; the test images were selected; skin tones under-represented
Rajpurkar et al., 2017 (CheXNet)[29] Pneumonia on ChestX-ray14; 121-layer convolutional network; test set of 420 images labelled by four radiologists F1 score above the average of the four radiologists Radiologists reading the same frontal images without clinical history Training labels mined from reports with known errors;[3] single institution; wide confidence intervals on 420 images
McKinney et al., Nature 2020[30] Breast-cancer screening mammography: 25,856 women in the UK and 3,097 in the US, with cancer status from follow-up Fewer false positives and negatives than the original readers; outperformed six radiologists in a reader study Historical first-reader decisions; a reader study of six radiologists Haibe-Kains et al. replied that code, model and data were not shared, so the result cannot be reproduced or audited;[31] retrospective
Ardila et al., Nat Med 2019[32] Lung-cancer screening on low-dose CT from the National Lung Screening Trial: 3-D network on whole volumes; cancer confirmed by biopsy AUC about 0.94 on 6,716 cases; fewer false positives and negatives than six radiologists when no prior CT was available Six radiologists, with and without the prior scan Trial data of a single country and era; small independent validation; no prospective use
Liu et al., Lancet Digit Health 2019[33] Systematic review of deep learning versus health-care professionals on medical images: 82 of more than 30,000 studies met the inclusion criteria Pooled sensitivity about 87 % versus 86 % and specificity about 93 % versus 91 % on the few studies with a fair comparison Clinicians, in the 14 studies that compared both on the same external sample Only 25 of 82 studies validated externally; few reported confidence intervals; the evidence base is poor

Three patterns run through the table. The reference standard is a human judgement or a biopsy, never the model’s own training labels, and the most credible papers used several readers and an adjudication. The comparator is almost always radiologists reading images without the clinical context they would have in practice, which favours the machine. And none of the original papers was prospective: the strongest claim any supports is “on retrospective images from these sources, the model’s operating point is comparable to these readers”, which is where Topol’s 2019 review placed the evidence.[34] The vocabulary of this course — sample, label, leakage, external validation, prevalence, confidence interval, shortcut — is sufficient to read every one of these papers critically.

Bridge to Unit 9

Unit 9 returns to these systems from the side of deployment: how a classifier becomes a diagnostic system with a user interface, a workflow and a monitoring plan; what data mining of the electronic record adds to imaging; and the professional-ethics questions that Sections 7.1–7.4 raised in technical form. The experiments of this unit — the topology grid, the shift test, the shortcut and its occlusion map — are the evidence you will be asked to produce in that discussion.

9. Summary

You should now be able to explain, without notes:

  • What a pixel value encodes in radiography, CT (Hounsfield units), MRI, ultrasound, histopathology, dermoscopy and retinal photography; why CT values are comparable across scanners and MRI values are not; what windowing, bit depth and DICOM are.
  • Why an image is a matrix and a feature vector at once, what flattening discards (adjacency), and the five stages of the imaging pipeline.
  • What min–max scaling, standardisation, histogram equalisation (and the algorithm behind it), resizing, Gaussian denoising and augmentation do, and the label-preservation condition that governs augmentation.
  • How to compute first-order, GLCM texture and shape features; how to trace a co-occurrence matrix and its contrast, homogeneity and energy by hand; why designed features beat raw pixels with a thousand images.
  • How a perceptron classifies flattened images, how to estimate its accuracy with repeated stratified cross-validation, how to read its confusion matrix and its first-layer templates, and how to choose a threshold for a screening prevalence.
  • The four rules of an honest topology experiment, what the depth × width grid, the learning curves and the penalty/activation/optimiser experiments showed, and why nested cross-validation is needed to report the result.
  • Why a perceptron is not translation-invariant, how to trace a convolution, a ReLU and a max-pooling by hand, and why convolution plus pooling plus augmentation generalises to shifts that augmentation alone does not.
  • What shortcut learning is, how to reproduce it with a hospital marker, how an occlusion-sensitivity map reveals it, and why external validation, stratified evaluation and saliency inspection are the defences.
  • Why accuracy is meaningless under class imbalance, what label noise does to a model and to its measured accuracy, and what the regulatory record says about how imaging AI has been evaluated.
  • How to read a landmark paper: objects, labels, reference standard, sample, metric, comparator, and what is missing.

What is simulated here, and what the Python edition did differently

R bundles no handwritten-digit or medical-image dataset, so this unit builds both of its image sources from code: a 6-class set of 8 × 8 glyphs in place of the Python edition’s handwritten digits, and 16 × 16 radiograph-like patches in place of its 32 × 32 patches. The numbers therefore differ from the Python notebook, but every qualitative conclusion is the same. One language difference shapes Section 5: R’s nnet offers a single logistic hidden layer optimised by BFGS, so depth was studied with neuralnet (on a PCA representation, for convergence) and the learning-rate/momentum/batch experiment was run on a from-scratch gradient-descent trainer with a rectified-linear activation. The union of these three tools covers the ground the single Python MLPClassifier covered.

10. Self-assessment

  1. A CT voxel has the value −850 and an MRI voxel has the value 850. What can you say about the tissue in each case, and why is the answer different in kind?
The CT value is in Hounsfield units, a physical scale: −850 is close to air, so the voxel is most likely aerated lung. The MRI value is in arbitrary units that depend on the scanner, coil and pulse sequence; by itself it says nothing, and only its relation to other voxels of the same acquisition is informative. This is why MRI requires per-image intensity normalisation and CT uses windowing.
  1. Trace the histogram equalisation of a 2 × 2 image with values (0, 0, 1, 3) on a 4-level scale.
Histogram: level 0 occurs twice, level 1 once, level 2 never, level 3 once. Cumulative distribution F: F(0) = 2/4 = 0.5, F(1) = 0.75, F(2) = 0.75, F(3) = 1. New value in [0,1] is F itself (or rescaled to the level range). The two dark pixels map to 0.5, the 1 maps to 0.75 and the 3 to 1: the image’s values are pushed up and spread, and the contrast between the two dark pixels disappears — equalisation of a tiny image is coarse.
  1. In the augmentation chunk, which of the six transformations preserves the label of a chest radiograph classified for pneumonia? For a mammogram classified for laterality (left/right breast)? For a dermoscopic image classified for melanoma?
Pneumonia: all six preserve the label, though left–right flipping should be avoided if the model will also report the side. Laterality: the left–right flip destroys the label (it is the label), the others preserve it. Melanoma: all six, because a skin lesion has no canonical orientation or exposure.
  1. Compute the GLCM contrast of the 3 × 3 image [[0,1,0],[0,1,0],[0,1,0]] with 2 levels and the displacement “one pixel to the right”.
Horizontal pairs: each row gives (0,1) and (1,0), six pairs in all, all with |i − j| = 1. P(0,1) = P(1,0) = 1/2; contrast = Σ (i − j)² P = 1 · (1/2 + 1/2) = 1. Homogeneity = Σ P/(1 + |i − j|) = 1/2; energy = 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2. A vertical stripe pattern has maximal horizontal contrast.
  1. The perceptron of Section 4.1 reported an accuracy of (say) 0.93 ± 0.02 over ten splits. A colleague’s network scores 0.95 on one 70/30 split of the same data. Is it better?
Not demonstrably. The ten splits of our model ranged over several percentage points, so 0.95 is within the spread of a single split of the same model. A fair comparison trains both on the same repeated splits and compares the paired differences across folds; and if the colleague selected the architecture on that split, the 0.95 is optimistically biased (Section 5.6).
  1. In the depth × width grid the decisive jump was from the linear model to one hidden layer, while adding more layers changed the accuracy only within the fold-to-fold noise. Why should extra depth give so little reliable gain at this sample size?
A single hidden layer already makes the classes separable, so it captures most of the available signal and lifts accuracy far above the linear baseline. Each additional layer adds capacity, but with only a few hundred images that capacity cannot be constrained by the data, so any gain is small and uncertain (comparable to the standard deviation across folds) and the optimisation is harder because the gradient must pass through more layers. “Deep” helps when the data are large enough to constrain the extra parameters; with a small sample the experiment cannot demonstrate a depth benefit.
  1. Why is the best cell of a cross-validated grid not an unbiased estimate of the chosen model’s performance, and what estimate should be reported instead?
The best cell was chosen because it was the maximum of several noisy estimates on the same folds; the maximum of noisy quantities is biased upwards. The nested cross-validation estimate — the outer-fold accuracy of the procedure “choose by inner CV, then fit” — is unbiased for the deployed procedure and is what should be reported.
  1. Compute by hand the valid cross-correlation of [[2,2,2],[2,2,2],[0,0,0]] with the kernel [[1,1,1],[0,0,0],[−1,−1,−1]], then the result after ReLU.
The kernel is 3 × 3 and the image 3 × 3, so the output is a single number: 1·(2+2+2) + 0·(2+2+2) − 1·(0+0+0) = 6. ReLU(6) = 6. The kernel detects “bright above dark” and the image is exactly that, so the response is maximal. With the kernel flipped vertically the response would be −6 and the ReLU would give 0.
  1. In the shift table of Section 6.4, augmentation with one-pixel shifts repaired small shifts but not larger ones, whereas the convolutional front end with augmentation was robust to both. Explain the difference in one sentence each.
Augmentation taught the raw perceptron a few additional positions by rote, and a larger shift is a position it never saw; the pooled convolutional representation makes shifted images similar as vectors, so what the network learned from small examples transfers to larger shifts — the architecture supplies an inductive bias that the data alone did not.
  1. The model trained at hospital A had higher same-hospital accuracy than the marker-free model, yet it is the worse model. Which single evaluation would have shown this, and which diagnostic would have shown why?
Evaluation on patches from a different hospital without the marker (external validation) showed the drop; the occlusion-sensitivity map showed that the evidence used was the corner marker rather than the nodule.
  1. A classifier for a 5 % prevalence task reports 95 % accuracy. What is the least it could be doing, and which two numbers would you ask for?
Calling every case negative achieves 95 % accuracy with zero sensitivity. Ask for sensitivity and specificity (or the ROC curve), and then compute the PPV at the deployment prevalence; accuracy is not informative under imbalance.
  1. In the label-noise experiment, which curve would a researcher with noisily labelled data observe, and what does it imply for comparing a model against radiologists on such a test set?
The orange curve, measured against noisy test labels, which is capped near 1 − q. A model can appear far worse than it is, and a comparison with radiologists on the same noisy labels is distorted in a direction that depends on whether the radiologists’ errors correlate with the label noise. The remedy is a test set with an adjudicated reference standard, as the landmark papers used.

Glossary

Augmentation
Enlarging the training sample with transformed copies of its images (flips, rotations, shifts, intensity changes) under the condition that the transformation preserves the label; applied to training folds only.
Convolution (cross-correlation)
Sliding a small kernel over an image and recording, at each position, the sum of the products of kernel weights and underlying pixels; the output is a feature map. Deep-learning libraries compute the cross-correlation and call it convolution.
Convolutional neural network (CNN)
A network whose early layers are learned convolutions followed by non-linearities and pooling, so that the same feature detectors are applied at every position; the architecture of LeCun (1998) and of AlexNet (2012).
DICOM
Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine: the standard file and communication format of medical images, whose header stores acquisition parameters and patient data.
Equivariance / invariance (translation)
A representation is equivariant if shifting the input shifts the representation correspondingly, and invariant if the representation does not change; convolution is equivariant, pooling makes it locally invariant.
Feature map
The output of one kernel applied across the whole image; large where the image locally resembles the kernel.
Grey-level co-occurrence matrix (GLCM)
Haralick’s texture descriptor: the normalised counts of pairs of grey levels at a given displacement, from which contrast, homogeneity, energy and correlation are computed.
Histogram equalisation
Non-linear intensity mapping through the cumulative distribution of the image’s histogram, which spreads the grey levels over the available range.
Hounsfield unit (HU)
The CT intensity scale: 1000 (μ − μwater)/(μwater − μair), so that water is 0 and air is −1000; a physical quantity comparable across scanners.
Inductive bias
The assumptions built into a model’s architecture or training that let it generalise beyond the exact cases in the sample; convolution and pooling encode the assumption that the class does not depend on position.
Label noise
Errors in the training or test labels; uniform noise degrades a model mildly but caps the measured accuracy at about 1 − q; systematic noise is learned as if it were signal.
Learning curve
Cross-validated and training accuracy plotted against the number of training examples; the diagnostic for deciding whether more data or a different model is needed.
Nested cross-validation
An outer cross-validation that estimates the performance of a procedure in which the model configuration is chosen by an inner cross-validation on the training folds only.
Occlusion sensitivity
A saliency map obtained by covering successive regions of the image and recording the drop in the predicted probability of the class.
Pooling (max-pooling)
Replacing each block of a feature map by its maximum (or mean), which reduces the map’s size and discards the exact position of the feature within the block.
Radiomics
The computation of large standardised sets of first-order, texture and shape features from segmented lesions, followed by classical machine learning.
Reader study
An evaluation in which clinicians and the model read the same cases under comparable conditions; the standard comparator in the landmark papers.
Shortcut learning
A model’s reliance on a spurious regularity of the training data — a marker, a border, a scanner texture — that predicts the label there but not elsewhere.
Template (first-layer weights)
The weight vector of a hidden unit reshaped to the image size; it shows the pixel pattern to which the unit responds most strongly.
Transfer learning
Reusing a network pre-trained on a large dataset (ImageNet) by replacing its last layer and fine-tuning on a smaller medical dataset.
Windowing
Mapping a chosen interval of CT values to the displayed grey scale, clipping values outside it; different windows show lung, soft tissue or bone on the same slice.

Textbooks

  • James G, Witten D, Hastie T, Tibshirani R. An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in R. 2nd ed. Springer; 2021. — The R companion to the whole course; free PDF at statlearning.com.
  • Goodfellow I, Bengio Y, Courville A. Deep Learning. MIT Press; 2016. — Chapter 9 (convolutional networks) is the reference for Section 6; Chapter 7 for regularisation and early stopping; Chapter 8 for the optimisers of Section 5.5. Free online at deeplearningbook.org.
  • Bishop CM. Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning. Springer; 2006. — Chapter 5 for the multilayer perceptron, including the invariance and convolution discussion.
  • Hastie T, Tibshirani R, Friedman J. The Elements of Statistical Learning. 2nd ed. Springer; 2009. — Chapter 7 for model assessment and the bias of model selection; Chapter 11 for neural networks. Free PDF.
  • Gonzalez RC, Woods RE. Digital Image Processing. 4th ed. Pearson; 2018. — Chapters 3 and 10 for histogram equalisation, filtering and segmentation.

Online resources

  • CRAN Task View: Machine Learning & Statistical Learning — cran.r-project.org/view=MachineLearning; the catalogue of R packages for the methods of this unit.
  • MedMNIST — medmnist.com; small, standardised medical image datasets; the recommended next step after this notebook (with a deep-learning framework).
  • ISIC Archive — isic-archive.com; public dermoscopic images and the yearly melanoma classification challenges.
  • DICOM standard — dicomstandard.org; the oro.dicom R package reads DICOM files.
  • CLAIM checklist — pubs.rsna.org/page/ai/claim; the reporting checklist of Section 7.4 in its current version.
